- label "Say the shock"
- text input (id "shock-sentence", Enter submits) plus a button "Read the sky" that calls parseTypedShock with the current input

- Q1: [your question with a recommended default]

# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

6: /**
7:  * Console state (Phase E2): one boot, one selected account, one twist.
8:  * The store holds only what is genuinely shared and asynchronous; every
9:  * derived number (shock result, verdict band, plan text) is computed in
10:  * ConsoleView with useMemo from pure lib functions, so the store never
11:  * carries a second copy of the math and no selector can drift from the
12:  * card it renders.
13:  *
14:  * E6 judge mode reserves these keys (NOT wired in E2, no listeners here):
15:  *   R           reset the twist, keep the account
16:  *   Shift + R   reset everything, account included
17:  *   1 to 4      play shock preset layoff, cost_spike, emergency_repair, combo
18:  *   /           focus the account lookup input (id="account-lookup")
19:  *   Esc         clear the lookup query
20:  *   N           open a random account from the id index
21:  * When E6 lands it will read and write this same store, which is why the
22:  * preset buttons already carry data-preset attributes and every button is
23:  * type="button" (no form, no accidental submit).
24:  */
25: 
26: export type BootStatus = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'ready' | 'error'
27: 
28: export interface ConsoleState {
29:   /** Boot lifecycle: idle before the first attempt, error with a message. */
30:   status: BootStatus
31:   /** Human readable boot failure, null unless status is error. */
32:   error: string | null
33:   /** The parsed profiles artifact, null until the boot succeeds. */
34:   bundle: ProfilesArtifact | null
35:   /** Raw lookup text, exactly what the judge typed. */
36:   query: string
37:   /** Selected account id, validated against bundle.byId. */
38:   selectedId: string | null
39:   /** The live twist, always normalized. */
40:   twist: Twist
41:   /** The preset matching the twist field for field, else null. */
42:   activePresetId: PresetId | null
43:   /** Idempotent boot: one fetch, retry only after a failure. */
44:   boot: () => Promise<void>
45:   setQuery: (query: string) => void
46:   /** Accept an id only when it exists in the bundle. */
47:   selectAccount: (id: string) => void
48:   applyPreset: (id: PresetId) => void
49:   /** Merge a partial twist, normalize it, then re match the preset. */
50:   setTwistField: (patch: Partial<Twist>) => void
51:   /** Back to no shock, account kept. */
52:   resetTwist: () => void
53:   /** Back to an empty console: no account, no query, no shock. */
54:   resetAll: () => void
55: }
56: 
57: function messageOf(cause: unknown): string {
58:   return cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : String(cause)
59: }
60: 
61: function matchPreset(twist: Twist): PresetId | null {
62:   for (const preset of SHOCK_PRESETS) {
63:     if (sameTwist(normalizeTwist(preset.twist), twist)) {
64:       return preset.id
65:     }
66:   }
67:   return null
68: }
69: 
70: export const useConsole = create<ConsoleState>((set, get) => ({
71:   status: 'idle',
72:   error: null,
73:   bundle: null,
74:   query: '',
75:   selectedId: null,
76:   twist: IDLE_TWIST,
77:   activePresetId: null,
78: 
79:   boot: async () => {
80:     const status = get().status
81:     if (status === 'loading' || status === 'ready') {
82:       return
83:     }
84:     set({ status: 'loading', error: null })
85:     try {
86:       const bundle = await loadSharedProfiles()
87:       set({ status: 'ready', bundle, error: null })
88:     } catch (cause) {
89:       // The shared memo already cleared itself, so the next boot retries.
90:       set({ status: 'error', bundle: null, error: messageOf(cause) })
91:     }
92:   },
93: 
94:   setQuery: (query) => {
95:     set({ query })
96:   },
97: 
98:   selectAccount: (id) => {
99:     const bundle = get().bundle
100:     if (!bundle || !bundle.byId.has(id)) {
101:       return
102:     }
103:     set({ selectedId: id })
104:   },
105: 
106:   applyPreset: (id) => {
107:     const preset = presetById(id)
108:     if (!preset) {
109:       return
110:     }
111:     set({ twist: normalizeTwist(preset.twist), activePresetId: preset.id })
112:   },
113: 
114:   setTwistField: (patch) => {
115:     const twist = normalizeTwist({ ...get().twist, ...patch })
116:     set({ twist, activePresetId: matchPreset(twist) })
117:   },
118: 
119:   resetTwist: () => {
120:     set({ twist: IDLE_TWIST, activePresetId: null })
121:   },
122: 
123:   resetAll: () => {
124:     set({
125:       query: '',
126:       selectedId: null,
127:       twist: IDLE_TWIST,
128:       activePresetId: null,
129:     })
130:   },
131: }))

247: ### Confirmation before apply
248: 
249: Nothing writes to app state until the presenter confirms the parsed
250: chips with one explicit click or Enter. The chips show each parameter
251: with a one click stepper for correction, plus a formula strip showing
252: income and spending in dollars so the presenter can verify against the
253: judge's hand calculation. The runway number does not exist until
254: confirmation. This is mandatory, not polish: a misparse visible to a
255: judge computing by hand is the worst failure mode.
256: 
257: ### Failure mode and timeout
258: 
259: - Timeout is AbortSignal.timeout(3000), a hard 3 seconds, then
260:   automatic fallback to preset cards.
261: - Preset twist cards are always rendered and always clickable. A mode
262:   badge next to the input reads "typed shock Gemini" or "preset
263:   cards".
264: - On 429, 403, abort, or network error: no retry on 429, the mode
265:   badge flips to preset cards, an inline note reads "Gemini
266:   unavailable, using preset cards", the storm animation continues into
267:   the preset apply, and total delay stays under 3 seconds.
268: - A hash cache makes repeated identical sentences free.
269: 
270: ### Key management
271: 
272: The key is already created with $25 of credits on the paid tier, so
273: free tier quota limits do not apply and content is not used for
274: product improvement under paid terms. It is stored as
275: import.meta.env.VITE_GEMINI_KEY, inlined into the bundle as expected
276: for a static site, never in a file under public/, and never printed in
277: the UI. HTTP referrer restriction is recommended: github.io, localhost,
278: and the final custom domain. Delete the key after Sunday submission.
279: 
280: ### UX timing budget (3 minute live twist)
281: 
282: The input row sits directly above the preset twist cards, labeled "Say
283: the shock". The storm front rolling in is the loading state (no
284: spinner, label "reading the sky"). Target latency is about 1 second,
285: hard cap 3 seconds. Stretch after P0 ships: the judge speaks the shock
286: via the browser Web Speech API at no extra API cost.
287: 
288: ### Effort and testing
289: 
290: - Core effort 5.5 to 7.5 hours: parser module 1.5 to 2, UI input row
291:   and chips 2 to 2.5, loading state 0.5 to 1, tests 1, key setup and
292:   smoke test 0.5 to 1. Stretch mic input adds 1 to 1.5 hours.
293: - Testing: vitest for the clamp table, percent detection, fallback on
294:   429 and abort, and the chip correction path, with mocked fetch. Log
295:   every response (sentence hash, latency ms, raw JSON, clamped JSON)
296:   to console.info so the write-up can quote a measured p50.
297: 
298: ### Fit with hard constraints
299: 
300: This is the "network allowed as a bonus, never a dependency" pattern
301: made concrete: the console is fully usable offline with preset cards,
302: and the typed path is the only code that touches the network. The
303: Gemini path reuses the E2 shock math unchanged, so the judge
304: definitions contract and the integer cents rule are untouched, and a
305: misparse can never reach state without the confirmation step.

Good. Notes:
- `rp-sr-only` utility exists (screen reader only class) — useful.
- `noUnusedLocals`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` strict.

Design plan (frontend-design skill): This is an add-on inside an existing instrument panel; I follow the existing cp design language rather than new identity. Palette: reuse cp tokens; gemini badge = --cp-band-watch (#8b7cf6).

Now, decide PendingShock import. Let me think again about what backend-dev will write. The contract for me says props `pending: PendingShock` without saying where it's exported. Backend-dev's contract probably says: "consoleStore exports interface PendingShock" or shockParse exports ShockSpec and store exports PendingShock. 

To be robust: I could import type from consoleStore AND that's it. If wrong, typecheck error which I report as parallel-work issue... but it might persist after backend lands (mismatch), breaking the build. Bad.

Alternative robust approach: define the type where I own it. In ShockChips.tsx:

```ts
/** Shape of the pending typed shock, matching the store contract. */
export interface PendingShock { ... }
```

and TypedShock imports `type { PendingShock } from './ShockChips'`. Structural compatibility: when backend's `pendingShock` (its own PendingShock type) is passed to ShockChips, TS checks assignability. Requirements: my spec fields all present with number types (backend: numbers, yes). sentence: string. intent: backend uses enum union of strings → assignable to string. confidence: same. summary: string. fixes: I omit it → fine (extra property allowed in assignment of a typed value).

But what if backend's spec fields are optional (`incomeFactor?: number`)? Then not assignable to required. The contract says all fields required in schema and validation ensures numbers. Should be required.

1. Judge confirms a typed shock → shockMode = 'gemini' (twist produced by Gemini).
2. Judge types another sentence → parse fails → typedStatus 'fallback', typedNote mapped, shockMode stays 'gemini'.
3. My badge, per my spec ("text 'typed shock Gemini' when shockMode === 'gemini'"), would show "typed shock Gemini" while the note says Gemini unavailable.

Architecture says: "On 429, 403, abort, or network error: ... the mode badge flips to preset cards, an inline note reads 'Gemini unavailable, using preset cards'".

Hmm, but semantics: shockMode = which path produced the LIVE TWIST. After a fallback following an earlier confirmed gemini twist, the live twist is still the gemini one — so "typed shock Gemini" badge arguably describes the twist source, not the input availability. Two readings:

A) Badge = input mode availability (architecture: flips to preset cards on failure).
B) Badge = source of live twist (backend's shockMode semantics).

Edge case: gemini-confirmed twist + later failed parse → badge stays "typed shock Gemini" + note "Gemini unavailable...". Is that a violation of my spec? My spec ties badge strictly to shockMode. Should I make the badge also show "preset cards" when typedStatus === 'fallback'? That deviates from the letter of my spec ("when shockMode === 'gemini'"). Hmm.

Design decisions: badge and reading label use existing uppercase utility type so they read as instrument markings; the formula strip reuses the plan-block teal treatment (provenance teal means "checked", which is exactly what the strip is); chips reuse `cp-label` and `cp-field__value` (tabular numerals) so no parallel value style was invented; `ShockChips` renders a fragment so its three blocks become grid children of `.cp-typed` and inherit its gap without an extra wrapper class; `SpecField` is imported from `shockParse` so chip fields cannot drift from the store's `adjustPendingShock` signature; all money strings come from `formatCents` on `shockFormula` output, with only percent and month display conversions precomputed before JSX.
